title: Audit Report for Legal Information Assistant (LIA)
author: Keith Porcaro · Dana Han · Madhavi Nambiar · Daniela Pereira Salas · Cher Qin · Lisette-Victoria San Pedro

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the need for selective, human-governed deployment and materially extends the cluster with a product-level audit showing how answer quality, guardrails, language access, accessibility, privacy, feedback and resource integration determine realised value in a public-facing legal-aid system. It also reinforces use-context-specific evaluation by warning against generalising from one evolving product.
qs: But this suggests that guardrails limiting LIA’s answers were not consistently effective during the audit period.

LIA is grounded by retrieval-augmented generation from vetted materials; it places lawyers ﬁrmly in the loop; it bakes in user-feedback mechanisms; and it is managed through recurrent optimization and targeted risk reviews.

st.t: Justice chatbots: Actionable help exceeds correct information
st.an: The LIA audit directly supports the cluster’s proposition that access-to-justice value depends on actionable, context-relevant assistance rather than plausible legal information alone. It documents insufficiently actionable custody guidance, missing links to existing legal-help resources, a mismatched eviction response, and only exploratory evidence that prompt changes may improve performance.
qs: LIA's later answers on child custody offer a basic overview of the custody process, but are insufficiently detailed and actionable.
Zero sessions included a link to LANC's own custody packet, even when users asked for it.

kp.k: Audit findings are product-specific and time-bound
kp.d: The Duke Law School audit manually reviewed and tagged every session in its supplied dataset, covering launch through December 18, 2024, with some supplementary observations from 2025. Technical and methodological limitations prevented exhaustive evaluation and grading of all queries. Findings concern the deployed product, including its resources and design, rather than the underlying model alone; some recommendations had already been implemented by publication.
qs: Our findings cover LIA interactions between launch and December 18, 2024.
We manually reviewed and tagged every session in our provided dataset.
While we hope this audit will be informative and beneficial for others, we caution against using this audit to draw generalized conclusions about AI.
In other words: not every finding here is attributable to the quality of an underlying LLM.

kp.k: LIA applies retrieval-augmented generation to public legal information
kp.d: LANC developed LIA with LawDroid and launched it in July 2024 to help users locate legal information. Its retrieval-augmented generation architecture matches queries against LANC-prepared resources and passes retrieved material to an LLM. The foreword, authored by LANC board chair Jeffrey M. Kelly, presents concise answers and the information–advice boundary as deliberate responses to mission and regulatory constraints, rather than purely technical limitations.
qs: LIA (Legal Information Assistant) is a chatbot that Legal Aid of North Carolina (LANC) has deployed to help users find relevant information for legal questions.
Architecturally, LIA relies on retrieval augmented generation (RAG).
As a Legal Services Corporation-funded organization, LANC must operate within strict case-acceptance rules and responsibly navigate the boundary between legal information and legal advice.

kp.k: Usage measurement is limited by abandonment and flawed analytics
kp.d: The audit reduced 16,077 exported sessions to 15,888 post-launch sessions and then 6,395 sessions containing user messages. It estimated 4,500–6,300 users, but inadequate visitor fingerprinting, duplicate sessions and unidentified testing prevented reliable unique-user counts. Embedded-site sessions had 63.5% abandonment versus 50.5% on LawDroid's page; explanations involving user expectations or testing remain hypotheses. Most interactions were short: 61.7% ended after one or two user messages.
qs: During the audit period, there were no more than 6,395 user sessions with LIA.
Based on the data that we have available, our best estimate is between 4,500 and 6,300 people have used LIA during the study period.
Because LIA does not have a dedicated test sandbox, it is not clear how many sessions are from genuine users.
Most LIA sessions are brief: 61.7% of sessions end after one or two user messages.

kp.k: Public demand exceeds the chatbot's resource coverage
kp.d: Approximately 3,810 sessions (59%) concerned available resources, while 2,611 (41%) included off-book questions; these categories overlap. Housing and custody dominated supported topics, while uncovered demand included divorce, benefits, employment and immigration. Approximately 1,839 sessions (29%) sought an attorney, LANC contact or service information. The audit interprets this demand as an opportunity to expand and better integrate existing resources, not as evidence that the chatbot already meets legal need.
qs: Approximately 3,810 (59%) sessions in the dataset contained questions related to LIA’s available resources.
Approximately 2,611 (41%) sessions contained questions that were not related to LIA’s available resources.

Approximately 1,839 (29%) sessions contained requests for an attorney, requests to contact LANC, requests to get to a specific person, or requests about LANC’s service offerings or eligibility requirements.

kp.d: Despite intended refusal of unsupported topics, LIA supplied information in more than half of off-book sessions directly from its foundation model rather than LANC resources. Accuracy assessment of these answers was outside the audit's scope. The auditors warn that users would likely attribute such answers to LANC and would not necessarily understand the significance of a 'general' information label.
qs: In more than half of off-book sessions, LIA provided some information on the topic requested.
This information was generated directly by LIA’s underlying foundation model and was not based on any resources that LANC provided.
Evaluating the accuracy of these generated messages was outside the scope of this audit.
People using LIA are likely to attribute its answers to LANC, regardless of whether LANC had any role in generating the answers.

kp.k: Housing answers omitted critical steps and misstated tenant rights
kp.d: Among 575 sessions beginning with the suggested eviction question, 320 received answers the auditors considered too basic; around 40% of recipients immediately abandoned their sessions. Even more comprehensive answers sometimes understated rent-bond requirements. In approximately 20% of relevant cases (~40/200), LIA suggested tenants might withhold rent over unrepaired conditions, which the report states is not permitted in North Carolina. Complex questions produced contradictory timing information or inappropriate mobile-home guidance.
qs: Yet more than half the time (320/575), LIA’s answer is too basic to be helpful.
About half of the more comprehensive answers understated or omitted information on the importance of the rent bond.
But in approximately 20% of cases (~40/200), LIA suggested that tenants might have the right to withhold rent if a landlord doesn’t make repairs.
As in other categories, LIA does best when providing simple overviews in response to basic questions, but struggles with more complex user questions.

kp.k: Custody guidance was often insufficiently actionable
kp.d: The custody evaluation reports 1,031 sessions, including 560 beginning with the suggested opening question. In 310 of these, LIA gave only a terse direction to submit a form and seek online Legal Aid help; approximately 200 recipients then abandoned the session. Only 110 custody sessions linked to an NC Courts page, and none linked to LANC's custody packet. May 2025 synthetic tests showed that requests for more detailed explanations could elicit fuller answers and useful links, supporting a recommendation to adjust prompts.
qs: LIA's later answers on child custody offer a basic overview of the custody process, but are insufficiently detailed and actionable.
Zero sessions included a link to LANC's own custody packet, even when users asked for it.
Adjusting LIA's underlying prompts may help deliver better answers about child custody.

kp.k: Domestic violence support weakened with freeform questions
kp.d: The auditors judged LIA's basic protective-order explanation clear and correct, but found inconsistent referrals: 13 sessions linked to NCCADV and 29 included National Domestic Violence Hotline information. Freeform questions tended to receive less actionable responses, sometimes omitting how to initiate proceedings, immediate protection or relevant housing assistance. A handful of examples confused civil no-contact orders with domestic violence protective orders.
qs: People who ask freeform questions about domestic violence tend to receive worse answers.
While these answers rarely contain incorrect information, the person receiving them is usually left to Google next steps on their own.
Just 29 included information about the National Domestic Violence Hotline.

kp.k: Source maintenance and retrieval failures undermined legal accuracy
kp.d: LIA failed to retrieve available small-claims complaint-form information and never linked to LANC's English or Spanish small-claims guide. In 111 sessions, its fee wording misleadingly suggested defendants owed the $30 service fee. Name-change answers frequently misstated adult limits and parental-consent exceptions; the audit links these failures to outdated, overlapping resources and recommends regular legal updating. Consumer resources likewise required better organization and broader coverage.
qs: In 111 sessions, LIA misstates the fee structure to make it sound like the defendant must pay a $30 fee.
Of the 21 sampled sessions where LIA provided a relevant answer, just five included accurate information about how many times someone can change their name.
This failure is likely due to LIA’s outdated resources on name changes.
LANC needs to improve processes to ensure that materials are regularly up to date with changes in law.

kp.k: Disaster assistance exposed inconsistent guidance and capability claims
kp.d: LIA accurately supplied FEMA application information and deadlines but struggled with more complex benefits and insurance questions. For post-Helene housing problems, similar queries received different coverage of time-sensitive lease-termination options. It generated a sample notice in one session but refused an email-drafting request in another. In an isolated case, it promised to pass website corrections to LANC instead of directing the purported FEMA employee to contact LANC.
qs: LIA struggles to consistently surface these scenarios to users, seemingly including or omitting them at random.
LIA accurately described where to apply for FEMA assistance and the deadline for applying.
Rather than suggesting the user contact LANC directly, LIA promised to pass the corrections on itself, and prompted the user to share more details about how the webpage could be updated.

kp.k: Referral failures obstructed access to human legal help
kp.d: LIA generally could provide a phone number and application link but struggled with LANC service scope, eligibility, office details and case follow-ups. Approximately 400 requests for help finding an attorney received an incongruous advice refusal. Custody responses contradicted one another about LANC assistance, and pro bono requests frequently led to the volunteer page rather than a route for obtaining help.
qs: In general, LIA struggled to answer questions about LANC beyond providing a phone number and a link to apply online.
In approximately 400 cases, LIA incongruously responds to requests for help finding an attorney with “I cannot give advice”.
When people using LIA ask for pro bono help, LIA frequently redirects them to LANC’s pro bono volunteer page instead.

kp.k: Suggested questions and links introduced additional service failures
kp.d: Approximately 30% of user messages were suggested by LIA. Across 357 sessions, at least 563 suggested questions were subsequently refused. In 387 sessions, LIA supplied links absent from its provided resources, which does not itself establish that every such link was fabricated; 85 sessions contained broken or dead links. Non-clickable URLs appeared in 176 sessions. The audit also identified bugs or technical irregularities in approximately 253 sessions (3.9%).
qs: In total, approximately 30% of messages sent to LIA are suggested by LIA.
In at least 563 instances across 357 sessions, LIA refused to answer a question it suggested.
In 387 sessions (24.8% of sessions with links), LIA generated links that we did not find in the provided resources.
In 85 sessions, LIA generated broken or dead links.

kp.k: Sparse feedback cannot establish service quality
kp.d: LIA requested ratings in 785 sessions (12.2%), received 212 ratings, and obtained 61 written comments: 29 positive, 30 negative and two mixed. The reported average star rating was 3.82. Because feedback depended mainly on an infrequently used session-ending button, the auditors recommend always-available feedback and additional surveys. Per-message thumbs-up/down feedback was implemented during the audit. They caution that satisfaction can reflect desired answers rather than accuracy.
qs: LIA asks for a star rating in just 785 (12.2%) sessions.
Just 61 out of 212 sessions left written feedback.
People may react negatively to bad news, or positively to elaborate fabrications that match their expectations.

kp.k: Language and accessibility barriers limited equitable access
kp.d: Only 67 of 6,395 sessions were in Spanish. During the audited period, English-only interface elements and disclaimers risked uninformed acknowledgements and navigation mistakes. Synthetic tests found Spanish opening-question answers generally weaker than English equivalents in several topics. Accessibility testing identified absent keyboard activation for the embedded chatbot, inadequate focus indicators and contrast, and difficulty saving or printing conversations. The foreword reports subsequent Spanish interface and disclaimer improvements.
qs: Of the 6,395 user sessions, just 67 (1%) were in Spanish.
This means that Spanish speakers may not know what they are agreeing to, what LIA is and isn’t capable of doing, or that information submitted to LIA will not be confidential.
When LIA is embedded on LANC’s site, it cannot be activated with a keyboard, and is excluded from keyboard navigation.
Users want to save LIA conversations but are unable to.

kp.k: Confidentiality and retention require protections beyond disclaimers
kp.d: The audit finds LIA's confidentiality disclaimer inadequate given potential or current clients, adverse parties and sensitive legal questions. It recommends clearer warnings, minimizing IP collection from nonusers, filtering personal information, reducing retained history and providing a quick escape mechanism. A session-identifier-dependent vulnerability could expose past conversations; the vendor reported fixing it in May 2025. Separately, the small number of imminent-harm cases and synthetic tests produced appropriate crisis-resource responses.
qs: Currently, LIA includes a disclaimer warning users that their chats may not be confidential or privileged.
But alone, this disclaimer is insufficient for the realities of how people use LIA.
By default, the embedded LIA script appears to be logging and storing IP addresses of every visitor to LANC pages, regardless of whether that visitor has interacted with LIA at all.
This bug was reported by the vendor as fixed in May 2025.
In the cases we did find, and in synthetic testing, we found that LIA appropriately responded with suicide prevention and crisis intervention resources.

kp.k: Auditing supports iteration rather than proving access-to-justice impact
kp.d: Kelly's foreword argues that early independent auditing, lawyer involvement and iterative governance offer a replicable approach for public-interest AI, and reports improvements and plans for a toolkit. The audit itself does not establish downstream legal outcomes or resolved legal need. It recommends closer integration with existing resources, potentially repurposing LIA for resource discovery or explanation, and using interaction data to understand unmet demand and adapt services.
qs: In other words, this document records a baseline, more so than LIA’s trajectory.
LIA only scratches the surface of demand for legal help in North Carolina.
LIA might be repurposed as a tool for finding specific resources, or for helping to explain complex sections in existing resources.
Tools like LIA can also help LANC build a more complete understanding of the demand for legal help in North Carolina, and adapt their resources and service offerings to meet it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The audit presents LIA as a potentially useful route to legal information and an instrument for understanding unmet demand, but finds that its early deployment often failed to provide actionable, reliable assistance. The foreword separately advances a more optimistic claim about responsible scaling through governance and iteration.
pts.d: The Duke audit authors claim that LIA performs best on basic overviews but struggles with complex or even mildly complicated questions. They identify inaccurate legal information, omissions of important procedural details, inconsistent refusals, ineffective retrieval of available resources, and inadequate assistance with contacting LANC. They report that LIA answered more than half of off-book sessions using its underlying model rather than LANC-provided resources, despite its intended restrictions. They attribute some failures to outdated or poorly organized source materials and product design, rather than treating them all as limitations of the underlying model. Their forward-looking proposals are that LIA could become a resource-finding or explanation tool and help LANC adapt its services to public demand. In the foreword, Jeffrey M. Kelly, identified as LANC board chair, claims that early independent auditing accelerated improvements and that LANC's approach can help other legal aid programs scale access responsibly. These are distinct from the audit's empirical findings and do not establish that AI replaces lawyers or improves legal outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The audit supports its product-specific claims with deployment records, manual session tagging, selected answer evaluations, synthetic testing, technical investigation, and resource review—not a general AI benchmark or a study of legal outcomes.
pts.d: The authors manually reviewed and tagged the supplied session dataset, then evaluated answers within subsets; they did not exhaustively grade every query. After filtering launch and onboarding records, they retained no more than 6,395 sessions, including unidentified tests and some duplicates. They estimated 4,500–6,300 users but could not determine unique users precisely. Approximately 59% of sessions included on-book questions, 41% included off-book questions, and 29% included contact requests; these categories overlap. Illustrative findings include approximately 40 of 200 relevant housing cases suggesting a possible right to withhold rent, 111 sessions ambiguously describing small-claims service fees as if defendants must pay them, 85 sessions with broken or dead links, and approximately 400 incongruous advice refusals in response to requests to find a lawyer. The authors also identify outdated name-change resources as a likely source of incorrect answers. Synthetic testing examined prompt changes, Spanish performance, accessibility, and safety. They did not evaluate off-book answer accuracy or establish whether users achieved better legal outcomes. Kelly's scaling and governance claims rest on the reported improvement process and institutional experience rather than quantified outcome or cost evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe an early deployment baseline from July–December 2024, supplemented by observations in 2025; proposed benefits depend on improvements to resources, interface design, safeguards, and governance.
pts.d: LIA launched in July 2024, with the session analysis beginning at its July 9 launch and ending December 18, 2024. The audit was conducted in a Duke Law School class in spring 2025 and includes later observations, including May 2025 prompt experiments. Findings were shared during the audit, and some recommendations were implemented before publication; per-message feedback was introduced during the audit, and the vendor reported fixing a conversation-access vulnerability in May 2025. The authors explicitly caution that the findings may not describe the current product and should not be generalized to AI overall. Future resource-navigation and demand-analysis uses are possibilities without a specified delivery date. Kelly's foreword, written approaching the pilot's first anniversary, describes continuing improvement and potential benefits from frontier-model advances. His account conditions responsible scaling on oversight, vetted materials, lawyer involvement, feedback, risk review, and attention to LANC's regulatory and mission constraints.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are North Carolinians seeking civil legal help, particularly people without lawyers, alongside LANC and other legal aid organizations considering similar systems.
pts.d: For tenants, parents, domestic-violence survivors, disaster-affected residents, and people facing consumer or name-change issues, the claimed opportunity is easier access to understandable legal information and relevant resources. The observed risks include misleading legal information, missing deadlines or procedural requirements, poor referrals, and continued movement between websites, phone lines, and the chatbot without obtaining help. Spanish speakers face English-only onboarding and warnings, inconsistent Spanish answers, and limited translated downstream resources; disabled users face keyboard, contrast, printing, and link-access barriers. Sensitive disclosures and retained conversations create confidentiality and safety concerns for current or prospective clients, people in conflict with LANC clients, and survivors vulnerable to monitoring. LANC faces responsibility for answers users may attribute to it even when those answers were not grounded in its materials. It may also gain better information about unmet demand. Other legal aid programs are the intended beneficiaries of Kelly's proposed transferable governance and implementation toolkit. LawDroid is the development vendor, not an alternative provider delivering the underlying legal representation.
